1233.title: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening (Shankara's commentary, 1.1.1–1.1.4)
1233.hook: someone hunts the whole house for the glasses on top of their head. Shankara asks how you can look for what you already have
1233.carry: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening (Shankara's commentary, 1.1.1–1.1.4)
1233.tomorrow: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening (Shankara's commentary, 1.1.1–1.1.4)
1233.howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta, students study Shankara's commentary on the first sutra with a teacher, and the question of what the self is runs through their reading, reflection and meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana and Shankara's preface: the I and the this, mixed up like silver seen on a shell.

Drawers are open. Couch cushions are on the floor. Someone has checked the car twice. Where are my glasses? Then a family member, trying not to laugh, points at the top of their head. The glasses were there the whole time. The searching was real, and it was also strange: you can't exactly find what you never lost, and you can't search for something you've never heard of. Shankara puts this puzzle at the start of the Brahma Sutra's very first line: now, therefore, the wish to know Brahman. Wait, he says. Is Brahman already known, or not? Either answer seems to stop the inquiry before it starts.
screen: `CUSHIONS ON THE FLOOR.` → `THE GLASSES WERE ON YOUR HEAD.` → `KNOWN, OR NOT KNOWN?`

segments.voice: If Brahman is already well known, why inquire? If it's wholly unknown, how could you even want to know it? You can't wish for what you have no idea of. His answer is quiet and surprising. Brahman is known, in a way, because it is the self of everyone. Nobody, he says, ever thinks, I am not. So the bare fact is never in doubt. What's in doubt is what this self is, and there people disagree widely. He lists the views. Some take the self to be the body, alive and aware. Some say it's the senses. Some, the mind. Some, a flicker of awareness, new each moment. Some say there is a self that acts and enjoys, apart from the body. Some speak of a Lord, separate from the self. Shankara lays these out as the views he will answer, and gives his own: the self is Brahman itself. Why does it matter? Take hold of a mistaken view without examining it, he says, and you might miss the highest good. So the inquiry is worth the effort, leaning on reasoning that serves the Upanishads. Notice what that does to jnana. It isn't finding a new object, like a coin. It's closer to the glasses: on his reading, nobody ever lacks the self, only clarity about it. Other Vedanta schools honor the same opening line and say what the self is differently. Here, Shankara speaks.
screen: `KNOWN, OR UNKNOWN?` · `NOBODY THINKS: I AM NOT.` · `MANY VIEWS OF THE SELF.` · `NOT FINDING, BUT CLARITY.`

segments.voice: Notice that you are here; you don't need to prove it or name it. Let the mind offer its labels one at a time, this body, these senses, these thoughts, and let each pass without deciding anything. Come back each time to the plain sense of being here, before any label; if you pray, offer that plain presence.
Jnana. Knowing. On Shankara's reading of the first line, not finding something new, but becoming clear about a self that is never lacking.
Your line: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening, Shankara's commentary, one point one point one to one point one point four. Not a coin to find, but glasses already on the head. I'll be here tomorrow.

1234.title: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening (Shankara's commentary, 1.1.1–1.1.4)
1234.hook: a tall shape in the fog: a person, or a post? you can guess either way, but only one guess is knowing
1234.carry: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening (Shankara's commentary, 1.1.1–1.1.4)
1234.tomorrow: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening (Shankara's commentary, 1.1.1–1.1.4)
1234.howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta, study of the Upanishads with a teacher is followed by reflection and meditation, so that what is heard becomes direct understanding.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana as clarity: nobody thinks I am not, yet people disagree about what the self is.

Early morning, thick fog, a walk along a field. Up ahead, something tall stands at the edge of the path. A person, waiting? A fence post? Decide it's a person, and your heart speeds up. Decide it's a post, and you keep walking. You could change your mind three times. None of that changes what is standing in the fog. When you get close enough, the thing itself settles the question. Shankara uses this very kind of example, a post that might be a man, while commenting on the Brahma Sutra's second line.
screen: `A SHAPE IN THE FOG.` → `PERSON, OR POST?` → `THE THING SETTLES IT.`

segments.voice: The second line says Brahman is that from which the birth and the rest of this world come. Shankara asks a sharp question. If that describes a cause, couldn't someone just reason their way to it? See a world, infer a maker, done. Not on its own, he says. The line gathers the Upanishads' own sayings, and reasoning is welcome only as their helper, because Brahman is not something the senses can show you. Then the post. With action, he says, a person has choices: you can do a ritual, skip it, or do it another way. Duty depends on the one who does it. Knowing isn't like that. Of one post in the fog, you can think post, or man, or something else, but only one of those thoughts is knowledge; the others are just opinions. Knowledge depends on the thing. And since Brahman is something that already is, not something to be done, knowing it depends on Brahman, not on anyone's choosing. That's why, he says, this knowledge doesn't end in words alone; it is meant to culminate in direct experience. So jnana, in Shankara's hands, is the opposite of a mood or a preference. It's the moment the fog thins and the question settles itself. Not every school draws the line between doing and knowing where he does. Ramanuja, for one, joins knowing to loving meditation. Shankara draws it here, firmly.
screen: `NOT A STAND-ALONE ARGUMENT.` · `DOING HAS CHOICES.` · `KNOWING DEPENDS ON THE THING.` · `MEANT TO END IN EXPERIENCE.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes rest on one plain object near you: a cup, a door handle, the edge of a table. Notice the opinions that rise about it, nice, ugly, needs cleaning, and let them go by like fog. Come back each time to the object itself, its shape and color, just as it is; if you pray, offer this attention as it is.
Jnana. Knowing. For Shankara, knowing that depends on the thing itself, not on anyone's choosing, and that is meant to end in direct experience.
Your line: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening, Shankara's commentary, one point one point one to one point one point four. Only one thought about the post is knowledge. Go gently.

1235.title: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening (Shankara's commentary, 1.1.1–1.1.4)
1235.hook: "visiting relatives can be boring" means two things at once. the Brahma Sutra's third line does too, and Shankara keeps both
1235.carry: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening (Shankara's commentary, 1.1.1–1.1.4)
1235.tomorrow: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening (Shankara's commentary, 1.1.1–1.1.4)
1235.howItsDone: Vedanta schools treat the Upanishads as the means of knowing Brahman, so their students study these texts closely, often with a teacher and alongside a commentary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana and the post in the fog: doing has choices, but knowing depends on the thing.

Visiting relatives can be boring. Hear that one more time. Is it boring to go and visit them? Or are the relatives who come to visit you the boring ones? The words don't change. The meaning flips. Often a sentence like that is a small accident. But a very short text, packed as tight as a seed, can carry two meanings on purpose, or at least leave room for both. The Brahma Sutra's third line is tiny. Shankara reads it two ways, one after the other, and doesn't throw either away.
screen: `VISITING RELATIVES CAN BE BORING.` → `SAME WORDS, TWO MEANINGS.` → `A SHORT LINE, READ TWICE.`

segments.voice: The third line says, in effect: because of being the source of scripture. The key word is yoni: a source, a womb, a place things come from. And the compound can be read in two directions. First reading: Brahman is the source of scripture. Shankara points to the great Vedic texts, the Rig Veda and the rest, which shine on all kinds of things like a lamp. Texts like that, he says, can only come from something all-knowing; a source always knows more than what flows from it. He leans on the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, where the Vedas are described as the breathing out of a great being, as easily as breath. Second reading: scripture is the source, meaning the way of knowing Brahman. Here the line answers yesterday's worry. The senses can't reach Brahman, and reasoning alone can't settle it. So how is it known? Through the scriptures, the Upanishads above all. Scripture is the doorway by which jnana arrives. Shankara gives one reading, then the other, and lets both stand: one says where the texts come from, the other what they're for. Other Vedanta schools comment on this line in their own ways. For a jnana path, the double reading carries a quiet lesson: the source of what is known and the means of knowing it may be closer than they look.
screen: `YONI: A SOURCE, A WOMB.` · `BRAHMAN, THE SOURCE OF SCRIPTURE.` · `SCRIPTURE, THE WAY TO KNOW BRAHMAN.` · `BOTH READINGS STAND.`

segments.voice: Breathe naturally and notice the out-breath, the way it leaves without effort. Then notice the small pause before the next breath begins, and rest your attention there, at the source, where the breath hasn't started yet. Don't hold the breath; just notice the turning point, again and again, and if you pray, let each out-breath be an offering.
Jnana. Knowing. On the third line, Shankara finds two directions: Brahman as the source of scripture, and scripture as the way jnana arrives.

1236.title: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening (Shankara's commentary, 1.1.1–1.1.4)
1236.hook: a kid on tiptoe against the height chart can't earn being taller. on the fourth line, Shankara says freedom isn't earned either
1236.carry: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening (Shankara's commentary, 1.1.1–1.1.4)
1236.tomorrow: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening (Shankara's commentary, 1.1.1–1.1.4)
1236.howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta, good action and devotion are often understood as preparing the mind, while freedom itself is understood as coming through knowledge of the self.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana and the third line read twice: Brahman the source of scripture, scripture the way to know Brahman.

At the doctor's office, a kid backs up against the height chart on the wall. The nurse reaches for the little slider, and the kid's heels start to lift. Just a bit. Maybe it'll count. Everyone in the room smiles, because everyone knows: you can stretch, you can stand up straight, but you can't earn your height. You can only find out what it is. Shankara's comment on the Brahma Sutra's fourth line makes a point a lot like that, about the deepest thing a person can want. Freedom, he says, isn't the kind of thing you produce.
screen: `HEELS LIFTING AT THE HEIGHT CHART.` → `YOU CAN'T EARN YOUR HEIGHT.` → `THE LINE THAT BEGINS WITH BUT.`

segments.voice: The fourth line says, in effect: but that, because of samanvaya, because the texts are connected in it. Samanvaya means connection: the Upanishads fit together around Brahman. Now the small word but. Shankara says it turns away an objection, and he states the objection with care. It comes from thinkers in the Mimamsa school, who take the Veda with great seriousness. Their view: the Veda's sentences exist to tell people what to do, so the Upanishads must be about action too, perhaps a meditation to perform, or praise of the one who performs it. Shankara answers: the Upanishads teach Brahman, something that already is, not a task to be done. And his reason: anything produced by action has a beginning, and whatever begins also ends. A pot that's made can break. If freedom were the product of an action, it would end too. So freedom, moksha, can't be made. He sorts the results of action: making something new, reaching something, changing something, cleaning something. Freedom is none of these. It's what the self already is, eternally. What removes the obstacle is knowledge, jnana, the way light doesn't create the room; it shows it. Shankara isn't saying actions are pointless; for him, good action and devotion can make the mind ready. But the last step isn't a doing. Some other Vedanta schools see freedom as given by the Lord's grace, met by devotion. Here, Shankara speaks.
screen: `BUT: AN OBJECTION TURNED AWAY.` · `ARE THE UPANISHADS ABOUT ACTION?` · `WHAT BEGINS ALSO ENDS.` · `FREEDOM IS NOT MADE.`

segments.voice: Notice any small effort in the body, a tight jaw, a held belly, a leaning forward, and let each one soften. You don't have to make stillness; just stop adding effort and see what's already here. If the mind starts working at it, notice that too, and if you pray, rest in whatever you pray to, without asking.
Jnana. Knowing. On the fourth line, Shankara says freedom isn't produced by any action, so what frees is knowing what already is.
Your line: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening, Shankara's commentary, one point one point one to one point one point four. You can't earn your height; you can only find out what it is. Until tomorrow.

1237.title: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening (Shankara's commentary, 1.1.1–1.1.4)
1237.hook: a snake's shed skin lies on a rock, perfect and empty. Shankara borrows that image for the one who knows
1237.carry: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening (Shankara's commentary, 1.1.1–1.1.4)
1237.howItsDone: Advaita Vedanta teachers often read the Brahma Sutra's opening lines with students as a summary of the whole work, together with Shankara's commentary on them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana and the fourth line: freedom isn't made, so what frees is knowing.

On a warm rock beside a hiking trail lies a snake's skin. Whole. Every scale is printed on it, even the shape of the eyes. Hikers stop and lean in, a little thrilled and a little nervous. But the snake is long gone. What's left keeps the exact shape of a living thing, and nobody lives in it anymore. The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad uses that picture for the body of someone who has come to know. Shankara reaches for it near the end of his comment on the fourth line, and with it comes the last day on these four opening lines.
screen: `A SKIN ON A WARM ROCK.` → `THE SHAPE, AND NOBODY IN IT.` → `THE LAST DAY ON FOUR LINES.`

segments.voice: First, the four lines laid end to end. One: now, therefore, the wish to know Brahman. Two: that from which this world comes, stays, and goes. Three: because of being the source of scripture. Four: but that, because the texts are connected in it. A wish, a pointer, a source, a harmony. Some readers treat these four lines as the whole case in miniature. Now the image. The Upanishad says: as a snake's cast-off skin lies on an anthill, lifeless, thrown away, so lies this body. Shankara uses it to describe the one who knows. Being embodied, he says, comes from the old mix-up, the I taken for the body, the this taken for the I. When knowing removes the mix-up, the body doesn't vanish. It goes on walking, eating, getting tired. But it's no longer taken for the self. Like the skin on the rock, it keeps its shape, and nobody is trapped inside it. Then a test that's hard to forget. Someone who has truly understood, he says, no longer lives in the turning world the way they did before; someone who still lives in it exactly as before hasn't understood yet. Jnana, for him, isn't a theory you hold. It's a knowing that changes where you stand. Other schools read these lines differently; here, Shankara has had his say.
screen: `A WISH, A POINTER, A SOURCE, A HARMONY.` · `THE SNAKE'S CAST-OFF SKIN.` · `THE BODY NO LONGER TAKEN FOR THE SELF.` · `KNOWING CHANGES WHERE YOU STAND.`

segments.voice: Feel the whole body sitting, from the soles of the feet to the top of the head, and let the chair or the floor carry its weight. Feel where it touches down: heels, hands, the back of the legs. You don't need to push the body away; just let it rest, like something set down, and if you pray, offer the body's weight.
Jnana. Knowing. For Shankara, the knowing that removes the mix-up and changes where you stand, as a snake leaves its skin behind.

Your line: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening, Shankara's commentary, one point one point one to one point one point four. The shape stays on the rock, and nobody is trapped inside it. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1238.title: the Mandukya Karika (Gaudapada)
1238.hook: every night runs awake, then dreaming, then sleep with no dreams at all. a very short Upanishad, and Gaudapada's verses on it, start right there
1238.howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta the Mandukya Upanishad is traditionally studied together with Gaudapada's karika and Shankara's commentary, and Om is often chanted at the start and end of Hindu prayer and study.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed six days of jnana with Shankara on the Brahma Sutra's first four lines, and a snake's skin left on a rock.
screen: `JNANA: THE SKIN ON THE ROCK.` · `FOUR LINES, SIX DAYS.`

segments.voice: Every night has the same itinerary. First, awake: lights, phone, the sound of the street. Then the room fades, and there's somewhere else entirely, a conversation with someone who isn't there, in a house nobody owns. Then even that goes, and there's deep sleep, where no world shows up at all. By morning the trip is over, and it starts again the next night. Three rooms, one night. A very short Upanishad, the Mandukya, first met back in year one, builds its whole teaching on those three rooms, and on a fourth. Verses written on it, tradition says by a teacher named Gaudapada, are called the Mandukya Karika.
screen: `AWAKE. DREAMING. DEEP SLEEP.` → `EVERY NIGHT, THE SAME TRIP.` → `THREE ROOMS, AND A FOURTH.`

segments.voice: The Mandukya Upanishad opens with a sweeping line: all this is Om. Then it says the self has four quarters. The first is waking, turned outward, enjoying the world of solid things. The second is dreaming, turned inward, enjoying a world made of the mind. The third is deep sleep, where nothing is wanted and no dream is seen, a gathered mass of awareness, full of ease. And the fourth, turiya, which simply means the fourth, is described almost entirely by what it is not. Not turned inward, not turned outward, not a mass of awareness, not knowing, not unknowing. Peaceful. Not two. That, the Upanishad says, is the self, the one to be known. Then it lays the sound of Om over the map. A is waking. U is dreaming. M is deep sleep. And the fourth has no letter; some readers hear it in the silence after the syllable ends. Gaudapada's karika, his explanatory verses, take this tiny text and think it through. Tradition places him in Shankara's own lineage, the teacher of Shankara's teacher, and a commentary on these verses is traditionally ascribed to Shankara. In his opening verses Gaudapada says the one self is known as three in the three states. And he sets the tone for all that follows: when a person sleeping in a beginningless dream wakes up, then the unborn, sleepless, dreamless, not-two is known.
screen: `ALL THIS IS OM.` · `WAKING, DREAMING, DEEP SLEEP.` · `TURIYA: THE FOURTH.` · `A, U, M, AND THE SILENCE.`

segments.voice: If you like, say Om once, softly or silently, and let the sound fade on its own; then rest in the quiet that follows, without filling it. When the mind starts talking, say Om again and rest once more in the quiet after it. If saying Om isn't part of your life, just listen to the room, and to the quiet between sounds; if you pray, let the silence be your prayer.

1239.title: the Mandukya Karika (Gaudapada)
1239.hook: a coil on a dim path makes a walker's heart jump. a flashlight shows a rope. Gaudapada asks where the snake went
1239.howItsDone: Advaita Vedanta teachers use the rope and the snake to explain how the world can be taken for something it isn't, and students reflect on the image in study and meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mandukya Karika opened: waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth, with Om laid over all of it.
screen: `THE MANDUKYA KARIKA: THREE ROOMS AND A FOURTH.` · `A WEEK TO LOOK BACK ON.`

segments.voice: A man is coming home late, down a dim side path. Something lies coiled across the stones. A snake. His body reacts before he can think: a jump, a cold flush, a step back. He finds his phone and turns on the light. It's a rope. He laughs, a little too loud. And then, if he's the kind of person who wonders, a strange question arrives. Where did the snake go? It made his heart pound; it was real enough for that. Gaudapada asks this question in the Mandukya Karika, and his answer reaches back across the whole week.
screen: `A COIL ON THE PATH.` → `THE LIGHT: A ROPE.` → `WHERE DID THE SNAKE GO?`

segments.voice: First, the week. Six days with Shankara on the Brahma Sutra's first four lines, and his word jnana, the knowing that undoes a mix-up. Then Gaudapada's verses on the Mandukya, with its three states and the fourth. Today the two threads meet, because tradition places Gaudapada before Shankara, in Shankara's own lineage, and the mix-up gets a vivid picture in his verses. One section of the Karika asks how real the world people see is. He starts with dreams. Inside a dream there are cities, roads, whole days of travel, and yet it all happens inside the sleeper. On waking, it's gone. Then the bold move: what isn't there at the beginning and isn't there at the end, he says, isn't truly there in the middle either. Now the rope. A rope, not seen clearly in the dark, is imagined as a snake, or as a stream of water, or as other things. When the rope is seen for what it is, the imagining stops. In the same way, he says, the self is imagined as all kinds of things, and when the self is known, the imagining ends. Notice what he doesn't say. The snake didn't turn into the rope, or crawl away. It was never anything apart from the rope. Gaudapada's reading is a hard one, and some other schools of Vedanta answer it: they hold the world to be real, the work of the Lord.
screen: `A WEEK OF JNANA, THEN THE MANDUKYA.` · `NOT AT THE START, NOT AT THE END.` · `THE ROPE TAKEN FOR A SNAKE.` · `THE SNAKE WAS NEVER APART FROM IT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small worry that has been coiled on your path this week. Don't push it away; look at it the way you'd shine a light on something in the dark, and ask gently: what is actually here? Then let the question rest and come back to the breath; if you pray, hold the worry up to the light you pray to.
The Mandukya Karika. Gaudapada's verses on the Mandukya Upanishad, where a rope seen in the dark as a snake stands for the self taken for all kinds of things.
Your line: the Mandukya Karika, Gaudapada. The snake never went anywhere; it was never apart from the rope. Until tomorrow.
